title: The vibe check
scenario: Lantern Studio makes product images for Fernhill Candles. It wants to know if a new image model can replace the one it uses now. You judge how the studio defines quality, using the exhibit. The studio, the plan and the numbers are made up for this case.
exhibit:
PLAN (made up for this case)
  Step 1  Run Model A (current) and Model B (new) on 40 prompts.
  Step 2  Look at both sets of images and decide what "good" means.
  Step 3  Pick the winner.
  Both are OpenAI GPT Image 2.5 models.

CRITERIA DRAFT (made up)
  1  Images look professional.
  2  Labels are right.
  3  Nothing unsafe.

TEST SET (made up)
  40 prompts written by the team while it built the prompt kit.
  Every prompt is simple: one candle on a plain table.
  None uses a long label, a dark background or a real client order.

SCORING (made up)
  The art director gives each image one overall score from 1 to 10.

TEST #17 (made up)
  Prompt: "Make a 4096x4096 hero image."
  Result: Model A failed 5 of 5 tries. Model B failed 5 of 5 tries.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with the order of the steps in the plan?

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because seeing real outputs first is the best way to learn what good means
options.explanation: Criteria written after the results can bend toward the model you already like. OpenAI lists vibe-based evals as an anti-pattern.

options.text: Step 1 needs far more prompts, because 40 is too few for any test to be useful at all
options.explanation: Anthropic says 20-50 simple tasks drawn from real failures is a great start. The order of the steps is the problem.

options.text: Step 2 comes after the results, so the criteria should be written down before the first run
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's process starts with defining the eval objective, and Anthropic says evals make teams specify what success means.

options.text: The plan needs a third model, because a test of only two models cannot show which is better
options.explanation: Two models can be compared. The weak point is that "good" is defined late.

questions.prompt: Which rewrite of criterion 2, "Labels are right", is the most measurable?

options.text: Labels are right in most images, as judged by whoever happens to look at them on the day
options.explanation: Most and whoever are both vague. Two people could give two different answers.

options.text: The label reads exactly "Fernhill Soy Candle" in at least 95% of test jobs, no extra letters
options.explanation: Right. It is specific and has a number, like Claude's good example of a share of outputs over a set number of trials.

options.text: Labels are right and look nice, and the art director is happy with them overall after a review
options.explanation: This mixes two ideas and ends in a mood. It has no target to measure.

options.text: Labels are as right as in a good photo shoot, so that nobody on the team has to worry
options.explanation: A comparison with a feeling is not a target. Claude asks for specific and measurable criteria.

questions.prompt: What is the main weakness of the test set?

options.text: It holds only easy prompts, so it does not mirror real orders or include hard cases
options.explanation: Right. Claude says to mirror your real-world task distribution and to cover edge cases. OpenAI warns against sets that do not match real traffic.

options.text: It is far too small, because every fair test needs at least 1,000 prompts to start
options.explanation: Anthropic says teams do not need hundreds of tasks to start. Too few hard cases is the problem.

options.text: It copies the real work too closely, because test prompts should differ from real briefs
options.explanation: The advice is the opposite. Claude and OpenAI both say the set should mirror real work.

options.text: It contains no prompts that Model B is good at, so the whole test is unfair to Model B
options.explanation: A test set should mirror the real job. It does not need to favour either model.

questions.prompt: The art director proposes one overall score from 1 to 10 for each image. What is the better design?

options.text: Keep one score, since a single number is the easiest thing to compare across two models
options.explanation: One number hides trade-offs. A model can look better and cost more.

options.text: Keep one score, but ask three reviewers and use the average of their quick first guesses
options.explanation: More reviewers do not fix a blended score. The criteria are still mixed together.

options.text: Use only the label criterion, because text is the one part of an image that can be measured
options.explanation: Claude says qualitative scales can be valuable when used consistently, along with numbers. Other criteria can be measured too.

options.text: Use several criteria with separate targets, and add cost and speed to the list as well
options.explanation: Right. Claude says most use cases need multidimensional evaluation, and its common criteria include latency and price.

questions.prompt: In test #17, both models failed every try. What is the best next step?

options.text: Report that neither model can make large hero images, so never use them for that job
options.explanation: That conclusion is too early. A test that every model fails may be a broken test.

options.text: Read the test first: 4096 is above the 3840-pixel edge limit that OpenAI lists for them
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic says a 0% pass rate is most often a sign of a broken task. OpenAI's guide caps each edge at 3840 pixels for its GPT Image 2.5 models.

options.text: Run the test 100 more times, until one of the two models finally gets one pass
options.explanation: More tries on a broken task only add noise and cost.

options.text: Drop test #17 and keep the other 39, without telling anyone that the test was cut
options.explanation: A removed test should be explained. The reason may point to a mistake in the test, not in the models.
